summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to supervise welding on a coded job. You will learn to check procedures and drawings, match every joint to a qualified welder, keep qualifications current, control materials and consumables, run hot work, confined-space and fume controls, check the work as it goes on, manage repairs and inspections, plan crew sizes and costs, lead and coach the crew, and keep the records that prove the job was done right.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **welding supervision**: making sure that welding on a job is done safely, by qualified welders, to the approved procedures and drawings, on time and at a fair cost, and that the records prove it.

At Level 3 you are no longer judged only on your own welds. You are judged on the work of the crew you lead: whether every joint went to a welder qualified for it, whether the consumables were controlled, whether the hot work was safe, whether problems were caught early, and whether the job file is complete at handover.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, leading hands and foremen in fabrication shops, and welders moving up to run a crew on site.

What this means on the job
rows: Prepare the job
Read the drawings, specification and inspection and test plan; check that an approved WPS covers every joint; raise queries in writing.
Match welders to joints
Build a qualification matrix, check each welder's records and continuity, and give each joint only to a welder qualified for it.
Control materials, consumables and equipment
Keep materials traceable; receive, store, issue and return consumables under control; keep welding sets and leads safe and tagged.
Keep the work safe
Run hot work permits and fire watch, confined-space entry, fume and heat controls; stop unsafe work; deal with incidents.
Control quality as the work goes on
Check fit-up, preheat, settings, interpass temperature and cleaning against the WPS; manage hold points, tests and repairs.
Plan and improve output
Work out crew sizes and times, raise the operator factor, cut repair costs and waste.
Lead and develop the crew
Brief the crew, give toolbox talks, coach welders whose work falls off, and use trainees safely.
Record and report
Keep the weld map, logs and daily reports; write non-conformance reports; hand over a complete job file.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the supervisor's role, procedures, welder qualification, traceability, consumables, safety, quality monitoring, repairs, productivity, costs and records.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example operator factor, qualification matrix, continuity log, hot work permit, RFI, standby person, toolbox talk, issue log) and essays in full sentences, with any sums worked out.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: supervising a small coded welding job (matrix, briefing, consumable issue, in-process checks and a daily report), and a role play in which you deal with staged problems and record your actions.

blocks.note: Most theory questions ask what a supervisor should do **first** or **best**. The answer is nearly always the one that keeps the work safe and inside the written procedure, deals with the facts, and puts it in writing. Shortcuts that "save time" are the wrong answer.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A welding supervisor sees that welding is done **safely**, **to the WPS and the drawings**, by **qualified welders**, and that it is **recorded**. You may still weld, but your first job is to organise, check and lead. If something goes wrong on your shift, the question will be: did the supervisor plan for it, see it and act on it?

blocks.h: Before, during and after the job

head: Stage
What the supervisor does
rows: Before welding starts
Read the drawings, the specification and the inspection and test plan (ITP)
Check that an approved WPS covers every joint on the weld map
Check each welder's qualification and continuity, and build the qualification matrix
Check that materials and consumables are the right grade and traceable
Check that equipment is safe and in date, and that permits and safety controls are in place
Plan the welding sequence and the crew, and brief the welders
While welding goes on
Check fit-up, preheat, settings, interpass temperature, cleaning and consumable control against the WPS
Watch for unsafe acts and conditions, and stop them
Deal with problems and queries; call the inspector at hold points
Watch the repair rate by welder and act on it
Keep the daily report and the weld log up to date
When the welding is finished
See that all welds are inspected and tested as the ITP says
Close out repairs and re-tests
Leave the area safe; return unused consumables; close permits
Complete the records for the job file and hand over

blocks.p: Jamaica's workplace safety law places duties on employers, supervisors and workers. As the person in charge of a crew, you must **stop unsafe work when you see it and put it right**, not wait for the safety officer or the end of the week. You must also make sure your crew has the training, information and protective equipment the job needs. "The job was behind programme" is never a defence.

blocks.note: If you see a welder working unsafely, stop the work, explain the danger in plain words, put the control in place, and then let the work go on. Record it if it was serious or keeps happening.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Person
What they need from you
What you need from them
rows: Your manager or project engineer
Daily progress, problems, costs and anything that changes the scope
Decisions on changes, extra resources, written instructions
The design engineer
Requests for information (RFIs) when a drawing is unclear or cannot be built
A written answer or a revised drawing
The client's inspector
Notice when a hold or witness point is ready; access to records and to the work
Releases at hold points; inspection results
The testing company (NDT)
Welds clean, numbered and reachable; a safe, cleared area
Test results matched to the weld map
The storekeeper
Consumable needs in good time; issue rules
Controlled issue and logged returns
The crew
Clear instructions, safe conditions, coaching and fair treatment
Work to the WPS, honest reporting of problems

ul: Only the person with authority (usually your manager, with the engineer or client) can change a specification, a test or a WPS, and only **in writing**.
If a client's representative asks you to skip a test, change an electrode or accept a fault "to save time", refer it to your manager. Never record a test as done when it was not.
Your signature on a record means you saw it and it is true. Never sign for work you did not check.

blocks.note: Many small Jamaican shops do coded work only now and then, for a hotel, a factory, a utility or a government project. That is exactly when the paperwork gets forgotten. Treat every coded job as if the client's auditor will read every record, because they may.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Procedures, drawings and the job documents

blocks.p: A coded job is welded to a **code** (for example the AWS structural or pipe code, or another code the contract names) and a **specification** written for the job. The supervisor does not need to know every clause, but must know which documents control the work and where to find the answer.

head: Document
What it is
What you check
rows: Welding procedure specification (WPS)
The written instructions for making a weld: process, base metal and thickness range, joint design, filler, gas, current and polarity, position, preheat, interpass temperature, travel speed and so on
That there is an approved WPS for every joint type, and that the welders have it and follow it
Procedure qualification record (PQR)
The record of the test weld that proved the WPS works, with the actual settings and test results
That each WPS that needs one is backed by a PQR whose ranges cover the job. Some codes allow prequalified WPSs that need no test if they keep within the code's limits.
Welder qualification record
Proof that a welder passed a test on a stated process, position, material and thickness range, signed by the examiner
That it covers the joints you give the welder and is still current
Drawings
Sizes, joints, weld symbols, materials, notes
That the crew is working to the latest revision
Inspection and test plan (ITP)
A list of every inspection and test, when it happens, who does it, and whether it is a hold point or a witness point
That no stage goes past a hold point without release
Weld map
A drawing or list that gives every weld a number
That each weld's welder, date, consumable batch, preheat and test result are recorded against its number

head: Type
What it means
What you do
rows: Hold point
Work must **not** go past this stage until the named person (often the client's inspector) has inspected and released it
Give the notice the ITP says; plan other work while you wait; never cover the joint with the next pass until it is released in writing
Witness point
The named person must be **given notice** and may come to watch; if they do not come after proper notice, the work may go on
Give notice as the ITP says, record when and how you gave it, and carry on if they do not attend

ul: Each drawing carries a **revision** letter or number. Only the latest issued revision may be used on the floor.
When a new revision arrives, find out what changed, take the old copies out of use (mark them SUPERSEDED or remove them), and check whether any work already done is affected.
Never mark changes on an old drawing from memory or from a phone call.

blocks.h: When a drawing is wrong or unclear

blocks.p: If a weld cannot be made as drawn, sizes do not add up, or a detail is missing, send a **request for information (RFI)** to the engineer. An RFI states the drawing number and revision, the exact question, a sketch if it helps, and when you need the answer. Keep a log of RFIs and their answers. Do not let a welder "make it fit" by guessing.

flow: Spot the problem and stop work on that detail
Write the RFI: drawing, revision, location, question, sketch, date needed
Send it to the engineer through the agreed route and log it
Plan other work while you wait
Act only on the written answer or the revised drawing, and brief the crew on the change

blocks.note: A WPS is hard to read at the booth. Go through it with the crew at the job, and post a short **key-settings sheet** for each joint type (electrode or wire, size, current range, polarity, preheat, interpass limit) at the work station. The sheet must match the WPS exactly; the WPS stays the controlling document.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A welder's qualification proves he can make a sound weld with a stated **process**, in stated **positions**, on a stated range of **materials, thicknesses and diameters**. It does not prove he can weld anything. The supervisor's job is to give each joint only to a welder whose qualification covers it.

head: Variable
What to check
Typical rule (always check the code the job uses)
rows: Process
MMAW, GMAW, FCAW, GTAW, SAW
A test in one process does not cover another
Position
Plate: 1G–4G (groove), 1F–4F (fillet). Pipe: 1G, 2G, 5G, 6G
Harder positions cover easier ones. A 3G plate test does not cover pipe; a 6G pipe test usually covers most plate and pipe positions
Thickness
The test plate or pipe wall thickness
Often covers up to about twice the test thickness; a test on thick plate (often 25 mm or more) may cover any thickness
Pipe diameter
The outside diameter of the test pipe
Small-diameter tests have limits on what they cover
Filler metal
Electrode or wire type
A test with a harder-to-use electrode (for example low-hydrogen E7018) usually also covers easier groups, but not the other way round
Backing
With backing strip or open root
An open-root test usually covers welds with backing, not the reverse

blocks.note: When a case does not fit the table, look it up in the code's qualification tables or ask the welding engineer or inspector. Never "assume it's close enough".
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **qualification matrix** is a chart with every welder down one side and the processes, positions and thickness ranges across the top. Fill it in from the signed qualification records, then compare it with the weld map. Each joint goes only to a welder with a tick in the right box.

head: Welder (ID)
MMAW 3G plate up to 20 mm
MMAW 6G pipe
GTAW 6G pipe root
Continuity checked
rows: D. Brown (W04)
Yes
No
No
1 Nov
K. Ellis (W07)
Yes

blocks.p: In this example only W07 may weld GTAW pipe roots, and W04 must not be given 6G pipe joints. If there are more pipe roots than one welder can do, either plan the programme round W07, or arrange a **witnessed qualification test** for another welder before he works on them.

ul: Ask for the original qualification records before the welder starts, not after.
Check the record is signed by the examiner or inspector who watched the test, and that the range covers your joints.
Check the record is genuine and current: the name and ID match, and there is continuity evidence. If in doubt, contact whoever issued it, or test the welder.
A test record without an examiner's signature, or a photocopy that cannot be checked, is not proof.
The examiner or inspector watches the **whole** test, from fit-up to the last pass, to confirm it was made to the WPS without help.
The test piece is marked so it cannot be swapped, then inspected and tested as the code says.
The examiner signs the record. The welder's own signature, or a workmate's, does not qualify anyone.

blocks.p: Under many codes a qualification **lapses** if the welder has not used that process for a set time, often **six months**. A **continuity log** records, for each welder and each process, the last date he welded with it on qualified work. Check it at least monthly. A welder whose continuity has lapsed must not weld coded joints with that process until he is retested, or as the code allows.
A qualification can also be withdrawn when there is a clear reason to doubt the welder's skill, for example a run of rejected welds. Then he is retested before he goes back on coded work.

Each welder on a coded job has an **ID number or stamp**. He marks it beside each weld (with a paint marker or low-stress stamp, as the job allows), and it goes on the weld map. Every weld can then be **traced** to the welder who made it, which is how you find a pattern in faults and prove who was qualified.

ul: Trainees and welders without the right qualification may help with **uncoded** tasks: fit-up assistance, cutting, grinding, temporary attachments where the WPS allows, and practice on test pieces.
They do not make coded welds, not even a root pass, and a qualified welder cannot "sign for" their work.
Plan their path to qualification: practice, then a witnessed test.

blocks.p: On a coded job, every piece of steel must be traceable to its **mill certificate** (the steelmaker's record of its grade, chemistry and test results). The link is the **heat number** stamped or painted on the plate, pipe or section.

ul: When steel arrives, match the heat numbers to the certificates and to the grade on the drawing. Steel with no heat number or no certificate is kept apart (quarantined) until it is sorted out.
When a plate is cut, **transfer the heat number** onto every piece before the marked part is cut away, including offcuts that may be used for gussets, stiffeners or test plates.
Record the heat number of each part against the weld map or the material list.

blocks.h: Consumable control from delivery to return

flow: Receive: check class, size, batch (lot) number and certificate against the WPS and the order; packets sealed and undamaged
Quarantine anything doubtful: wrong class, damaged packets, no certificate
Store: dry, locked store, by type, off the floor, first in first out
Condition: low-hydrogen electrodes and flux in ovens at the maker's temperatures, with the oven temperature logged each shift
Issue: a named person issues against the WPS for each joint, in small amounts, and records it on the issue log
Use: welders keep low-hydrogen electrodes in heated quivers that are switched on
Return: unused electrodes back at the end of the shift; re-dry or scrap as the maker says; record it

head: Record
What it shows
rows: Receipt record
What arrived, batch numbers, certificates, any rejections
Oven log
Oven temperatures at set times each shift, and any power cuts or faults
Issue log
Which consumable and batch went to which welder, for which joint, when, and from which oven
Return record
What came back, and whether it was re-dried or scrapped

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air and power cuts are the enemies of low-hydrogen electrodes. After any power cut, check how long the ovens were off and treat the electrodes as the maker says (often re-baking) before you issue any. Record it in the oven log. A quiver that is not plugged in is just a box.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: What you notice
Check first
Action
rows: Gas use much higher than usual for the same work
Leaks at hoses, fittings and regulators; flow settings
Leak test, repair or replace, set flows to the WPS
Long electrode stubs in the bin
How short the welders burn their rods
Coach the crew to burn rods to a short stub (about 40–50 mm)
Wrong electrode at a booth
Issue log and the WPS for that joint
Stop the welding, hold the welds made, report, and fix the issue system
Wire or flux running out early
Over-welding (welds bigger than drawn), spillage, waste
Check weld sizes against the drawing; coach

ul: Each welding set, lead, holder and work clamp is inspected at set intervals and tagged with the date of the check.
Damaged cables, cracked holders and loose connections cause electric shock, burns, fires and poor welds.
A faulty set is switched off, isolated and given an **out-of-service tag** at once, and reported. Only the person named on the tag, or a competent person who has fixed the fault, removes it.
Check meters on sets used for coded work are in calibration, or check the current with a calibrated clamp meter, so the settings recorded on the weld log are true.

blocks.p: Safety is planned before the first arc, briefed to the crew, checked during the work and closed out at the end. As supervisor you set the standard: if you walk past an unsafe act, you have accepted it.

blocks.h: Hot work permit and fire watch

blocks.p: A **hot work permit** is a signed form that allows welding, cutting or grinding in a set place, at a set time, once the fire risks are controlled. It is issued by the person in charge of the site and closed when the work and the fire watch are over.

ul: Clear or cover anything that can burn for at least 10 metres; look above and below; cover gaps, drains and openings that sparks can fall through.
Extinguishers of the right type at the work, and people who know how to use them.

A **fire watch**: a person whose only job is to watch for fire during the work and for a set time after it, with an extinguisher at hand. The permit sets the time, often 30–60 minutes, because smouldering material can burst into flame later.
The fire watch checks the whole area, including below the work and behind walls and partitions.

blocks.p: Tanks, vessels, pits, large pipes and closed boxes are **confined spaces**. Air in them can lack oxygen, be enriched with oxygen, or hold flammable or toxic gas, and fume and heat build up fast. First ask: can the work be done from outside?

head: Control
Why
rows: Confined space entry permit and hot work permit
The space is formally checked and controlled before anyone goes in
Isolation from pipes, power and moving parts
Nothing can flow in or start up while people are inside
Gas test with a calibrated **gas detector** before entry and during the work (oxygen, flammable gas, toxic gas)
Conditions change: leaks, fume and purge gas
Forced ventilation and fume extraction
Fresh air in, fume out; **never** use oxygen to "freshen" the air: oxygen-rich air makes clothing burn fiercely
Gas cylinders and welding sets outside; hoses and torches taken out at breaks
A leak inside the space can cause fire or suffocation
A **standby person** at the entrance, in contact with the welder, who does not leave or go in
Raises the alarm and starts the rescue plan
A rescue plan and equipment ready before entry
Rescuers without equipment become casualties too
Low-voltage lighting, heat breaks, suitable PPE and RPE
Shock, heat stress and fume are worse in a small space

ul: Fume hanging in a bay means the controls are not working. First improve the **extraction** (move hoods close to the arc, clear blockages), then check the welders's **RPE** (respiratory protective equipment) is the right type, fitted and maintained.
Galvanised, painted and stainless work, and work in enclosed spaces, need extra controls.
RPE is the last line of defence, not the first.

blocks.p: Welders wear heavy PPE beside a heat source, often in the Jamaican sun or inside steel tanks. Plan the work for cooler hours where you can, give regular breaks in the shade, keep cool drinking water at the job, and watch for signs.

head: Condition
Signs
Action
rows: Heat exhaustion
Heavy sweating, headache, dizziness, cramps, weakness, feeling sick
Stop work, move to shade, loosen clothing, cool down, sip water; get medical advice if not better quickly
Heat stroke (an emergency)
Very hot skin, confusion, slurred speech, collapse; sweating may stop
Call 110 for an ambulance, cool the person fast with water and fanning, keep them in the shade until help comes

blocks.h: Electric shock, radiography and other trades

ul: After any electric shock, even if the welder says he is fine: stop the work, get him checked by a doctor or nurse, isolate and tag the set, and report it.
During **radiography** the crew stays outside the barriered area, as the radiographers direct. Plan it at night or at breaks, and never send anyone past the barrier.
Put up screens between welding and grinding, and direct sparks away from people.
Keep the public, guests and other trades out of reach of arc flash and falling sparks with screens, barriers and signs.

head: Condition
Risk
Control
rows: Wind
Shielding gas blown away (GMAW, gas-shielded FCAW, GTAW): porosity
Screen the joints, or use a process the WPS allows outdoors
Rain, wet steel, wet ground
Porosity, cracking, electric shock
Stop, or shelter and dry the joint (preheat to drive off moisture if the WPS says); dry boards to stand on
Strong sun
Heat stress; hot steel; machines overheating
Breaks, water, shade, cooler hours
Work at height
Falls, dropped objects, sparks falling on people below
Safe access and fall protection; barriers below
Site power or generator
Shock, fire
Earthed supply, protected cables, refuel engines only when stopped and cool

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short safety briefing (often 5–15 minutes) at the start of a shift or before a new task. Keep it to one or two hazards that matter today, show the control, ask questions to check understanding, and record who attended.
Quality is built in while the weld is made, not inspected in afterwards. The supervisor's **in-process checks** catch problems while they are cheap to fix.

head: Check
Against
How
rows: Fit-up: gap, root face, bevel angle, alignment, tack quality
WPS and drawing
Weld gauge, rule, square
Joint cleanliness
WPS (mill scale, rust, paint, oil, moisture removed)
By eye
Consumable
WPS for that joint; issue log
Packet label, rod markings, oven or quiver
Preheat
WPS minimum, measured where the WPS says (a set distance from the joint)
Temperature crayon or contact thermometer
Interpass temperature
WPS maximum (and minimum, where given)
Check before each pass; wait if too hot; record it
Current, voltage, travel speed, gas flow
WPS ranges
Machine meters (in calibration) or clamp meter; flowmeter
Cleaning between passes
WPS and good practice
All slag removed, defects ground out
Welding sequence
The distortion plan
Watch the order; check the job stays in line

blocks.note: If you find a joint welded without the preheat the WPS calls for, or with the wrong consumable, stop it, mark and hold the welds already made, and report them. They may need testing or cutting out. Do not let the welder "put it right on the next pass".
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Agree a welding **sequence** before starting: balanced welding about the neutral axis, back-step or skip welding on long seams.
On a long girder or frame, have two welders work opposite each other in step, not one side fully then the other.
Do not over-weld: a weld bigger than drawn adds shrinkage, time and cost.
Check the job at stages and adjust the sequence before it is too late.

blocks.p: The **repair rate** is the share of tested welds (or of tested weld length) that needed repair. Track it by welder, by joint type and by week.

head: Formula
Worked example
rows: Repair rate % = welds repaired ÷ welds tested × 100
6 repairs in 40 radiographed joints: 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = **15%**

blocks.p: A rising repair rate is a signal, not a verdict. Find the facts before you act.

flow: Collect the facts: which welds failed, which defect, which position, since when
Ask what changed: new machine, new consumable batch, new joint type, weather, long hours
Talk with the welder in private, without blame, and listen
Check his set, leads, consumables, fit-up and conditions; watch him weld against the WPS
Fix the cause: repair or recalibrate equipment, coach the technique, practise on test pieces
If the problem goes on, take him off coded work and arrange a retest
Have his recent work checked, record what you did, and follow his repair rate in the coming weeks
Mark the defect on the weld and record its type, size and position (inspection report or non-conformance report)
Check the repair is allowed, and how many times, under the code or contract
Get the repair procedure approved and choose a welder qualified for it
Remove the defect by grinding or gouging; check the excavation (often with PT or MT) to prove it is all gone
Shape the groove so it can be welded well; apply preheat if the procedure says
Weld the repair to the repair procedure
Inspect and test again by the same method that found the defect
Record the result, welder and consumables on the weld map; close the report; deal with the cause

blocks.note: Repeated repairs on the same spot damage the steel. Codes and clients limit how many times one area may be repaired; after that the joint may have to be cut out and rewelded, or referred to the engineer.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Working with inspectors and testing companies

ul: Agree the ITP with the client's inspector before work starts, so everyone knows the hold points, witness points and tests.
Give notice in good time; have welds clean, numbered and reachable.
Make records available: WPSs, welder qualifications, consumable logs, preheat records.
When results come in, check them against the weld map, arrange repairs and re-tests, and track results by welder.
Stay polite and open. Record agreements in writing, and refer anything that changes the specification to your manager.

blocks.p: The **operator factor** (also called arc-on time or arc time ratio) is the share of a welder's paid time during which the arc is actually burning. The rest goes on fitting, cleaning, changing electrodes, moving, waiting and breaks.

head: Formula
Worked example
rows: Operator factor % = arc-on time ÷ paid time × 100
Arc on for 2 hours 48 minutes (2.8 h) in an 8-hour shift: 2.8 ÷ 8 × 100 = **35%**

blocks.p: Typical operator factors for manual welding are low, often about 20–40%, depending on the work. Raising the operator factor raises output without asking anyone to weld faster.

blocks.h: Ways to raise output without losing quality or safety

head: Lost time
What the supervisor can do
rows: Waiting for parts
Have fitters prepare and tack parts ahead of the welders
Fetching materials and consumables
Keep electrodes, wire, gas and tools at the work station; plan deliveries
Poor fit-up
Check fit-up before welding starts; a bad gap costs far more time to fill than to fix
Awkward positions
Use positioners and turning rolls so more welds are flat or horizontal: faster and fewer defects
Slow processes on long welds
Use a higher-deposition process (FCAW, SAW) where the WPS allows
Over-welding
Weld to the drawing size, no bigger: extra weld metal is extra time, cost and distortion
Repairs
Cut the repair rate with coaching and good conditions: a repair costs several times the original weld
Tired, overheated welders
Keep breaks and safe hours: tired welders make mistakes

head: Question
Method
Worked example
rows: How many welders?
Joints ÷ (joints per welder per day × days available), rounded up
72 joints in 6 days at 4 joints per welder per day: 72 ÷ (4 × 6) = **3 welders**
How many days?
Joints ÷ (welders × joints per welder per day), rounded up
90 joints, 3 welders at 5 joints each a day: 90 ÷ 15 = **6 days**
Days from arc time
Total arc hours ÷ (welders × shift hours × operator factor)
56 arc hours, 4 welders, 8-hour shift, 35%: 56 ÷ (4 × 8 × 0.35) = 56 ÷ 11.2 = **5 days**

blocks.note: Always round crew numbers and days **up**: 2.4 welders means 3 welders, and 5.2 days means 6 days. Then add time for inspection, hold points, weather and repairs.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Cost
How to work it out
Worked example
rows: Labour on a job
Hours × hourly rate
14 hours at J$2 200 an hour = J$30 800
Labour on a repair
Repair hours × hourly rate
2.5 hours at J$2 200 an hour = J$5 500
Repairs over a period
Number of repairs × cost of each
6 repairs at J$5 500 = J$33 000, before re-testing and delay costs
Gas per hour
Cost of gas ÷ hours it lasted
J$12 600 of gas over 9 hours = J$1 400 an hour

blocks.p: The true cost of a repair is more than the welder's time: grinding, consumables, the second NDT test, delay to the programme, and sometimes the client's inspector's return visit. That is why preventing defects is the cheapest way to raise output.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, write the units (hours, joints, J$) at each step, and check the answer makes sense: a crew of 40 welders for a 60-joint job is a slip of the calculator.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Leading the crew, records and reporting

blocks.p: Before a coded job starts, brief the whole crew at the job, not in the office. Cover:

ul: The job, the drawings (and their revision), and the weld map: who welds which joints
The WPS for each joint type and the key settings sheet
The welding sequence and distortion controls
Hold points and witness points: where work must stop for the inspector
Hazards and controls: permits, fire watch, confined spaces, fume, heat, work at height
Consumable issue and return rules
Roles: who fits, who welds, who keeps fire watch, who to tell when something goes wrong

blocks.p: Ask questions to check people understood. Record who attended.

ul: Praise in public; correct in private. Warning a welder in front of the crew makes people hide problems.
When a good welder's work suddenly falls off, talk first and check his set, consumables and conditions before thinking about a retest.
Coach one point at a time, show it, let him practise on a test piece, then check.
Plan trainees' progress: uncoded tasks, practice, then a witnessed test.

blocks.p: Write a daily report every shift. It is the job's diary, and it protects you and the firm if there is a dispute later.

blocks.p: When work does not meet the drawing, WPS, code or specification, record it on a **non-conformance report (NCR)**: what the requirement was, what was found (with measurements and a sketch or photo), where it is, and who found it. Mark and hold the item. The authorised person decides what happens to it (rework, repair, use as it is with a written concession, or scrap), and the NCR is closed only when the action is done and checked.

head: Record
Why it is kept
rows: Approved WPSs and their PQRs
Show every weld was made to a proven procedure
Welder qualification records, matrix and continuity log
Show every welder was qualified and current
Material certificates with heat numbers
Show the steel is the grade drawn and can be traced
Consumable certificates, oven and issue logs
Trace each weld's filler to its batch
Weld map with welder, date, consumable and results for each weld
Ties everything together
Inspection, NDT and repair records; NCRs
Show every weld passed, and how faults were closed
Daily reports, permits and toolbox talk records
Show the job was run safely and as planned

blocks.p: These records go into the **job file** (often called the data book) for the client. Later, if a weld fails in service, they let the firm trace it to its welder, materials and tests and find the cause. They also help price and plan the next job.

blocks.note: Write records at the time, in ink or in the job's system, and never fill them in from memory at the end of the week. A record written later is easy to challenge and hard to defend.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can describe a welding supervisor's duties before, during and after a coded job.
I can explain my legal duty to stop unsafe work.
I can check that an approved WPS covers each joint, and explain what a PQR is.
I can explain the difference between a hold point and a witness point.
I can deal with a new drawing revision and raise an RFI.
I can build a qualification matrix and give each joint only to a qualified welder.
I can check new and agency welders' records, and explain why a test must be witnessed.
I can keep a continuity log and explain when a qualification lapses.
I can keep materials traceable by heat number, including offcuts.
I can control consumables from receipt to return, with oven and issue logs.
I can run a hot work permit and fire watch, and plan confined-space entry with a standby person.
I can control fume, heat stress, shock risks and radiography safety for my crew.
I can check fit-up, preheat, interpass temperature and settings against the WPS.
I can work out a repair rate and deal fairly with a welder whose repairs rise.
I can manage a weld repair from finding the defect to closing the report.
I can work out operator factor, crew size, days and repair costs.
I can give a pre-job briefing and a toolbox talk.
I can write a daily report and an NCR, and list what goes in the job file.

terms: Welding done to a named code and specification, with approved procedures, qualified welders, inspection and records
A record of when each welder last used each process, to keep qualifications current
The set of welding and inspection records handed to the client
A person who watches for fire during and after hot work, with an extinguisher at hand
An instrument that tests air for oxygen level, flammable gas and toxic gas
The number on steel that links it to its mill certificate
A stage that must not be passed until the named person releases it
A signed form allowing welding, cutting or grinding in a set place and time once fire risks are controlled
The temperature of the joint just before the next pass; the WPS sets limits
A record of which consumables went to which welder, when, and from which oven
Inspection and test plan: every inspection and test, when, by whom, and whether it is a hold or witness point
Non-conformance report: a record of work that does not meet the requirement, and what is done about it
The share of a welder's paid time during which the arc is burning
A tag on faulty equipment that stops anyone using it
Procedure qualification record: the test record that proves a WPS
A chart of every welder against the processes, positions and ranges they are qualified for
Repaired welds as a percentage of welds tested
Request for information: a written question to the engineer about a drawing or specification
The person who stays outside a confined space, in contact with those inside, ready to raise the alarm
A short safety briefing at the start of a shift or task
Being able to link each weld to its welder, procedure, materials and tests
A drawing or list that numbers every weld on a job
A stage for which the named person must be given notice and may attend
Welding procedure specification: the written instructions for making a weld

c1.title: Pipe spools for a water treatment plant near Lionel Town
c1.text: Owen supervises a crew of four welding 40 carbon steel pipe butt joints for a water treatment plant near Lionel Town, Clarendon. The WPS calls for a GTAW root and an MMAW fill and cap with E7018. Delano's record shows a witnessed 6G pipe test with GTAW and MMAW, but the continuity log shows he last used GTAW on coded work in March; it is now November, and the code's limit is six months. Ricardo is qualified 6G for MMAW only. Tevin, a new welder, brings a photocopy of a 6G certificate from a past employer with no examiner's signature. Owen estimates about 1.4 hours of arc time per joint, with an operator factor of about 35% on 8-hour shifts.

c2.title: A packing-house extension in Hope Bay
c2.text: Shauna-Kay supervises three welders on the steel frame of a banana packing-house extension in Hope Bay, Portland, using MMAW with E7018. It is the rainy season, and at 10:00 a.m. a heavy shower soaks the steel and the ground. Bales of flattened cardboard cartons and a stack of wooden pallets stand about 6 metres from the nearest joint. The hot work permit asks for a 60-minute fire watch after the last hot work. The labourer named as fire watch has also been asked to fetch electrodes from the store when needed.

c3.title: Repairs rising at a trailer shop in Porus
c3.text: A shop in Porus, Manchester, welds heavy trailer chassis to a client's specification, and a share of the butt welds is radiographed. Kerry-Ann, a good welder, had 1 repair in 30 radiographed joints last month and 6 repairs in 40 this month. All six defects are lack of side-wall fusion in vertical-up joints. Two weeks ago she moved to a new inverter set at the far end of the shop, on a 40-metre lead. Each repair takes about 2.5 hours of welder time at J$2 200 an hour, and each re-test costs J$4 000.

c4.title: Bridge girders at a yard near Duncans
c4.text: Andre supervises the welding of plate girders for a river bridge at a fabrication yard near Duncans, Trelawny. The WPS calls for E7018 electrodes, kept in a holding oven and issued to heated quivers. Over the weekend a power cut left the oven off for about 30 hours, and the oven log is blank for Saturday and Sunday. On Monday morning the storekeeper is about to issue electrodes as normal. A new delivery of E7018 has also arrived with no batch certificate. One welder admits his quiver, with about 20 electrodes in it, was left unplugged overnight.

c5.title: A water tank for a hotel in Discovery Bay
c5.text: Sophia's crew is building a steel water-storage tank for a hotel in Discovery Bay, St Ann. The inspection and test plan makes the fit-up of the shell seams a witness point, needing 24 hours' notice to the client's inspector. Sophia gave written notice on Tuesday morning for a Wednesday morning inspection, but on Wednesday the inspector has not come or called. Later, the client's engineer, walking the site, tells her to make the nozzle fillet welds 10 mm instead of the 8 mm on the drawing.

questions.q: What should Owen decide about Delano welding the GTAW roots?
o: Let him weld them, as his 6G test covers every position on the job
Keep him off GTAW roots until he is retested or the code allows
Let him weld one root under watch, then carry on if it looks good
Let him weld them as long as Ricardo checks each root afterwards
questions.why: His test covers the positions, but continuity has lapsed: he has not used GTAW on qualified work for more than six months. Under the code he must not weld GTAW coded joints until he is requalified, however good he is.

questions.q: How should Owen treat Tevin's photocopied certificate?
o: Accept it, because a 6G test covers every joint on this job
Accept it once Tevin signs a note saying that it is genuine
As unproven: check it with the issuer, or test Tevin first
Let Tevin start on roots while Owen phones the old employer
questions.why: A qualification record must be signed by the examiner who watched the test and must be checkable. Until it is confirmed with whoever issued it, or Tevin passes a witnessed test, he does not weld coded joints.

questions.q: About how many working days should Owen plan for the crew of four to weld all 40 joints?
o: About 2 days
5 days
7 days
20 days
questions.why: Total arc time is 40 × 1.4 = 56 hours. Each welder gets about 8 × 0.35 = 2.8 arc hours a day, so the crew gets 11.2: 56 ÷ 11.2 = 5 days. Leaving out the operator factor gives the far too short 2 days.

questions.q: How can Owen make good use of Ricardo on these joints?
o: Have him run the GTAW roots too, since a root is a root in any process
Use him only for grinding, as one welder must weld each whole joint
Have him weld whole joints by MMAW and note the WPS change himself
Fill and cap behind a qualified root welder, both IDs on the weld map
questions.why: Where the WPS and code allow more than one welder on a joint (most do), each welds only the part his qualification covers. Both welder IDs go on the weld map so every pass can be traced. Only an authorised person changes a WPS.

questions.q: The shower has passed. What should Shauna-Kay do before welding starts again?
o: Restart at once, as E7018 is a low-hydrogen rod made for damp weather
Restart, but turn the current up so that the water boils off
Weld only the joints that are no longer dripping with water
Dry the joints (warming them if the WPS says) and give dry footing
questions.why: Water on the joint puts hydrogen into the weld and causes porosity and cracking, and wet ground and gloves raise the shock risk. Joints are dried, by warming where the WPS says, and welders stand on dry boards.

questions.q: What should be done about the cardboard bales and pallets before hot work starts?
o: Move them more than 10 m away, or cover them with fire blankets
Leave them where they are, since 6 m is well clear for arc welding
Weld only while the breeze is blowing away from the bales
Stand an extinguisher by the bales and carry on as planned
questions.why: Sparks and spatter travel 10 metres or more, further from height, and can smoulder in cardboard and wood. Combustibles are moved beyond that distance or covered with fire-resistant blankets; the extinguisher is an extra control, not a substitute.

questions.q: What is wrong with the fire watch arrangement?
o: A labourer is not senior enough to act as a fire watch on site
A fire watch must not leave the area or take on other duties
A fire watch is only needed after the welding, not during it
The fire watch should be one of the welders, who knows the job
questions.why: A fire watch's only job is to watch for fire during and after the hot work, with an extinguisher at hand. Sending them to the store leaves the area unwatched just when a spark may land.

questions.q: The last weld is finished at 3:30 p.m. When may the fire watch end and the permit be closed?
o: At 3:30 p.m., as soon as the last arc goes out
At 4:00 p.m., since 30 minutes is the usual minimum
At 4:30 p.m., after a final check of the whole area
The next morning, when the crew comes back to work
questions.why: The permit sets the time: 60 minutes after the last hot work here. The watch ends with a final check, including below and behind the work, and then the permit is closed with the person who issued it.

questions.q: What is Kerry-Ann's repair rate this month?
questions.why: Repair rate = repairs ÷ joints tested × 100 = 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = 15%. Dividing by 30 (last month's total) or by the 34 that passed gives the wrong answers.

questions.q: What should the supervisor do first about Kerry-Ann's repairs?
o: Send her for a requalification test before she welds again
Give all her vertical joints to other welders and say nothing
Talk with her in private and check the new set's real current
Have every one of her joints radiographed from now on
questions.why: Her record was good until she changed sets, and lack of fusion often comes from low current. A long lead and an unchecked new machine can deliver less than the dial shows, so check it with a clamp meter and hear her view before deciding anything else.

questions.q: About what did this month's six repairs cost in labour and re-testing?
questions.why: Each repair costs 2.5 × J$2 200 = J$5 500 in labour plus J$4 000 to re-test, J$9 500 in all. Six repairs cost 6 × J$9 500 = J$57 000, before counting delay and grinding.

questions.q: The manager wants to warn Kerry-Ann in front of the crew at Monday's toolbox talk. What is the best advice?
o: Speak to her privately; give the crew a general talk on fusion
Do it, as a public warning makes the whole crew take more care
Do it, but read out every welder's repair rate so it seems fair
Say nothing to anyone and wait to see if the rate falls on its own
questions.why: Correcting in private keeps trust and keeps people reporting problems. A general talk on avoiding lack of fusion helps everyone without shaming one welder, and the cause still has to be found and fixed.

questions.q: What should happen to the electrodes in the oven before any are issued?
o: Issue them: the closed oven kept the damp air out all weekend
Issue them for fill passes only, and keep new ones for roots
Scrap the whole oven load and order a full new supply
Re-bake them as the maker says and record it in the oven log
questions.why: After 30 hours without heat in humid air, the coating may have picked up moisture, and the blank log cannot prove otherwise. Re-baking to the maker's time and temperature restores them; the record shows it was done.

questions.q: What should Andre do with the new delivery that came without a certificate?
o: Use it, as long as the packets say E7018 on the label
Quarantine it, labelled, until a matching certificate arrives
Use it on the less important joints until the certificate comes
Send it back to the supplier at once without telling anyone
questions.why: On a coded job every consumable batch must be traceable to its certificate. Doubtful stock is kept apart and labelled so it cannot be issued by mistake, and the problem is reported to purchasing.

questions.q: What should happen to the 20 electrodes from the unplugged quiver?
o: Use them first thing, before they can pick up more damp
Leave them in the quiver and simply switch it back on
Return them to be re-baked or scrapped as the maker says
Give them to the trainees for practice on coded test plates
questions.why: An unheated quiver lets low-hydrogen electrodes pick up moisture overnight. They go back to the store, are re-baked or scrapped as the maker allows, and the return is recorded so the issue log stays true.

questions.q: The inspector has not come for the witness point. What may Sophia do?
o: Carry on, recording when and how the notice was given
Stop all work on the tank until the inspector arrives
Ask one of her welders to witness it and sign the plan
Skip the fit-up check altogether to make up the time
questions.why: At a witness point the inspector must be given proper notice and may attend; if they do not, the work may go on. Sophia records the notice and her own fit-up checks. A hold point would be different: work must wait for release.

questions.q: How should Sophia deal with the engineer's spoken change to the nozzle fillets?
o: Make them 10 mm at once, since the engineer outranks her
Ignore it and weld to the 8 mm on the drawing without comment
Ask the welders to make them as large as they can manage
Ask for the change in writing, then brief the crew on it
questions.why: A change to a weld size must come as a written instruction or a revised drawing, so the records match the work and the WPS still covers it. She refers it through her manager if needed; she does not ignore it.

questions.q: At noon a welder working in a hot tank becomes confused and slurs his words; his skin is very hot and dry. What should the supervisor do?
o: Give him salt tablets and let him go back in after lunch
Call 110 and cool him fast in the shade with water and fanning
Let him rest in the shade and finish the job later if he feels better
Give him a cold soft drink and send him home on the bus
questions.why: Confusion with hot, dry skin points to heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency. Call an ambulance and cool him quickly while you wait. Afterwards, plan cooler hours, breaks and water for the crew.

questions.q: Which is the best toolbox talk before a crew starts welding galvanised handrails?
o: A 45-minute talk on every hazard in the safety manual
A notice on the board for the crew to read when they can
Ten minutes on zinc fume and its controls, with questions
A talk on Friday about any illness the crew had that week
questions.why: A toolbox talk is short and aimed at today's main hazard, here zinc fume and metal fume fever. Asking questions checks understanding, and an attendance list records who was briefed.

questions.q: A crew is welding 200 brackets onto a fixed frame, and many fillets are overhead. Which change would most raise output and cut defects?
o: Turn the current up so the overhead fillets go faster
Make each fillet bigger so that fewer passes are needed overall
Pay a bonus per bracket and drop the patrol checks
Use a positioner so most welds are made flat or horizontal
questions.why: Flat and horizontal welds are faster and give fewer defects than overhead ones. More current overhead causes sagging and repairs, bigger fillets waste time and add distortion, and dropping checks lets faults through.
